title: Exporting Internal Tuning Decisions as Public Configuration
pattern: An implementation forces callers to choose low-level heuristic values (caching sizes, retry intervals, timeouts, thread counts) that it can responsibly determine itself, exporting mechanism complexity upward under the guise of "flexibility" rather than exposing meaningful user policy.
why_bad: Callers, operators, and administrators must understand implementation details to choose values they are ill-equipped to select, producing heavy cognitive load, incomplete solutions, and brittle static settings that cannot adapt to runtime conditions and go stale as workloads or environments change. It is a direct failure of the class to hide its implementation details.
detection: Over-configuration case: configuration structs exporting dozens of micro-parameters, with more than 15 mostly opaque or undocumented fields as a review heuristic. Individual-knob case: a public API or initialization struct exposes a temporal, capacity, or performance setting that encodes an internal heuristic without a sound caller-owned decision behind it. Mechanism case: structs representing low-level mechanisms (network, cache, file I/O) export primitive numeric retry/cache/I/O tuning fields that expose static implementation choices. In every case, establish that the choice belongs inside the mechanism; a numeric type, a parameter count, or the word timeout alone does not prove misuse.
source: *John K. Ousterhout - A Philosophy of Software Design (2018)*, Chapter 8, "Example: configuration parameters".; Ousterhout, John K - *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018_2019, Yaknyam Press).pdf, Section 8.2.; John Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018), Chapter 8, "Example: configuration parameters", p. 193, 446-447.
